units.title: Architecture documents, generation differences and vendor peaks as bounds
outcomes: Explain which document answers which question: brief for system architecture, tuning guide for optimization, ISA for instructions, counter docs for measurement.
Contrast Ampere, Hopper and Blackwell on Tensor-Core formats, TMA, thread-block clusters and memory using the compute-capability tables.
Derive a vendor-peak bound from per-SM throughput times SM count times clock, and label every assumption that makes it a bound rather than a measurement.
units.why: A peak number is a ceiling, not a result. Reading the right document tells you whether a claim is even possible before you spend a day measuring it.

next.note: Turn the capability columns into a dispatch matrix with fallback.
Use the derived peaks as the speed-of-light bound.

study.title: Compute Capabilities: feature and specification tables
study.locator: Section 5.1.3, Tables 29 to 33: read the 8.6 column against the 9.0 and 10.x columns for Tensor-Core dtypes, TMA, thread-block clusters and shared memory; Section 5.1.1 for the runtime query triplet

study.title: Arithmetic instruction throughputs as peak sources
study.locator: Section 12.1.1, Table 5: the 8.6/8.9 column for 32-bit floating-point add, multiply and multiply-add (128 results per clock per multiprocessor); the note that throughputs are per multiprocessor and max theoretical

study.title: Hardware generations and the number-as-hypothesis rule
study.locator: Chapter 2, AI System Hardware Overview: The CPU and GPU Superchip, NVIDIA GPU Tensor Cores and Transformer Engine, and A Glimpse into the Future

study.title: Current-hardware map and Source Policy
study.locator: Section 6, Current hardware: follow one architecture entry to its ISA or tuning guide; Source Policy: vendor peak numbers are not performance measurements, and performance claims need hardware, workload, precision, baseline and correctness method
study.depth: Use the list only to find primary documentation. Do not cite the list itself for numbers.

focus: Brief, tuning guide, ISA and counter documents answer different questions. A peak in a brief is an upper bound; only a counter on your GPU is a measurement.
Capability tables group columns by compute-capability number (8.6, 9.0, 10.x), not by marketing name. A blank cell inherits the value to its left; it never means missing hardware.
Table throughputs are per multiprocessor and max theoretical, achievable only with specific instruction sequences. Multiply by SM count and clock, and count one multiply-add result as two operations.

Hopper adds TMA, thread-block clusters, FP8 Tensor-Core input and fourth-generation NVLink; Blackwell adds fifth-generation NVLink and Blackwell-only matrix instructions. New columns add rows; old guarantees stay.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the FP32 peak and the memory bandwidth bound for an 18-SM sm_86 card: \(18 \times 128 \times 2 \times 1470 \times 10^{6} \approx 6.8 \times 10^{12}\) FLOP/s from Table 5, and \(12 \times 14 \times 10^{9} = 168 \times 10^{9}\) bytes/s from the 96-bit bus at 14e9 transfers/s. Place the ridge point at \(\approx 40 \text{ FLOP/byte}\) and state why sustained clocks measure lower.
traps: Quoting a Table 29 Yes as performance. Availability is not speed; a Yes in the 8.6 and 9.0 columns can hide an order of magnitude.
Mixing GB with GiB when checking a bandwidth bound. The 168 GB/s datasheet figure is decimal gigabytes; divide measured bytes by time in the same unit.
Reading a B200 or H100 number as your result. A peak from another GPU bounds nothing on yours; re-derive with your SM count from `prop.multiProcessorCount` and your clock.

selfTest.q: Your GPU reports compute capability 8.6. Does it have an FP8 Tensor-Core input path?
selfTest.a: No. The 8.6 column of the Tensor-Core dtype table shows no FP8 input; FP8 appears in later columns. An FP8 claim for this card needs a fallback path, not a peak quote.

selfTest.q: Derive the FP32 peak of an 18-SM sm_86 card at the 1470 MHz boost clock from Table 5.
selfTest.a: Table 5 gives 128 multiply-add results per clock per multiprocessor for 8.6/8.9. \(18 \times 128 \times 2 \times 1470 \times 10^{6} \approx 6.8 \times 10^{12}\) FLOP/s, where the factor 2 counts the multiply plus the add. Sustained clocks under power and thermal limits measure lower, so this is a bound.

selfTest.q: Show the datasheet bandwidth arithmetic for the 6 GB card and state the unit.
selfTest.a: A 96-bit bus carries 12 bytes per transfer at 14e9 transfers/s, so \(12 \times 14 \times 10^{9} = 168 \times 10^{9}\) bytes/s, decimal GB/s. Compare against measured bytes per second in the same unit.

selfTest.q: A post reports 3 TB/s on a newer GPU and claims your kernel should reach half of it. What is wrong?
selfTest.a: A peak from another GPU is not your bound. Your card is bounded by 168 GB/s, so half of 3 TB/s is unachievable there; the comparison needs your hardware, your workload and your measured counters.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the per-kernel peak-bound table and ridge-point placement behind the Milestone E regime predictions.
units.stopWhen: You can derive both peaks and the ridge point for your GPU from the tables without notes, and you reject a cross-GPU peak comparison on sight.

fit.note: The capability tables, the Best Practices throughput table and Chapter 2 cover document reading, generation differences and peak bounds at explain depth.

units.title: AMD CDNA and ROCm vocabulary
outcomes: Map CUDA terms for compute, threading, on-chip memory, matrix units and profiling to their AMD CDNA and ROCm counterparts at vocabulary depth.
Distinguish the CDNA datacenter line from the RDNA graphics line and place Composable Kernel, AITER and HipKittens in the right software layer.
units.why: Portability starts with names. A bound, a fallback or a profile means nothing if compute unit, wavefront and shared memory are confused across vendors.

next.note: Carry the AMD terms into the capability matrix as portability limits.
Name non-portable constructs correctly in the reconstruction audit.

study.title: Composable Kernel programming model
study.locator: Repository README: the tile-based programming model, Tensor Coordinate Transformation and the four CK layers (Templated Tile Operators down to Client API); one tiled operator example from the supported-operations lists

focus: CDNA is the datacenter compute line; RDNA is the graphics line. An inference kernel targets CDNA vocabulary, never gaming numbers.

Composable Kernel describes kernels through composable tiles, layouts and pipelines in HIP C++; AITER ships ready inference operators; HipKittens is a tile abstraction. Match the layer before comparing terms.
AMD counter names follow hardware blocks: compute unit, shader pipe interpolator, texture cache per pipe and per channel. Read the MI350 counter families as a vocabulary list, not as values.

Pallas is a Triton-like DSL and the JAX kernel model for GPU and TPU backends; NKI is the tile-level model for NeuronCore. Both are separate programming models, not CUDA ports; note where each runs and stop there.
units.reproduce: From memory, write the CUDA-to-AMD term map for compute unit, thread group, on-chip memory, matrix unit, profiler and kernel language with one-line roles each, and state which AMD line each targets.
traps: Treating HIP as CUDA with renamed calls. Grid and block structure carry over, but wavefront size, occupancy rules and shuffle semantics need per-architecture checks against AMD documentation.
Reading an MI350 counter as portable. Counter definitions are per architecture; a CDNA 4 compute-unit counter means nothing on NVIDIA hardware or on older CDNA.
Citing RDNA gaming throughput for a CDNA inference bound. Different lines, different memory systems, different peaks.

selfTest.q: Which AMD line targets datacenter inference, and which two repositories supply its tiling primitives and inference operators?
selfTest.a: CDNA. Composable Kernel supplies tiling, layout and operator primitives; AITER supplies inference and transformer operator implementations.

selfTest.q: What does HipKittens add over writing HIP directly?
selfTest.a: A tile abstraction for AMD GPUs: decomposition and layout handled above raw threads, comparable in role to Triton or CuTe on NVIDIA.

selfTest.q: Name two MI350 counter families and the block each watches.
selfTest.a: Compute unit counters watch the compute units; texture cache per pipe and per channel counters watch the cache hierarchy. Command processor and shader pipe interpolator counters cover dispatch and scheduling.

selfTest.q: Where does Pallas run, and what is it?
selfTest.a: Pallas is a Triton-like DSL and the JAX kernel model for GPU and TPU backends. It is a separate programming model, not a CUDA port.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the dispatch and fallback defense names the AMD (CDNA and HIP) counterpart of each dispatched path.
units.stopWhen: You can name the CDNA line, the three AMD code layers and two counter families without notes, and explain why none of it executes on your NVIDIA card.

fit.note: Coverage failed for real AMD vocabulary: Lecture 10 stays at taxonomy level and never names ROCm or HIP, so the ROCm Composable Kernel repository fills that gap.

units.title: Capability matrices, fallback and compatibility tests
outcomes: Build a capability matrix for your kernels: minimum compute capability, required features and the runtime query that detects each.
Implement dispatch with a correct portable fallback and an explicit error on unsupported paths, tested on every branch.
Explain PTX compatibility and fatbin contents: what runs where, what JIT-compiles at load, and what fails.
units.why: A kernel without a capability contract fails at someone else's machine, not at your desk. The matrix decides before launch; the fallback keeps older hardware working.

next.note: The reconstruction inherits this dispatch contract.
The reproduction records the matrix and exercises every branch.

study.title: Runtime capability queries and feature targets
study.locator: Section 5.1.1: the runtime query triplet (`cudaDeviceGetAttribute` with `cudaDevAttrComputeCapabilityMajor`, the driver query and the NVML query); Section 5.1.2: architecture-specific versus family-specific features and compiler targets (baseline, family and arch-only)

study.title: Binary compatibility, PTX compatibility and JIT compilation
study.locator: Section 1.3.1 with Binary Compatibility, PTX Compatibility and Just-in-Time Compilation: what a fatbin carries, what compiles at load, and what fails on newer hardware

study.title: Dispatch and fallback contract
study.locator: Architecture constraints: dispatch never selects an unvalidated shape, dtype or device path, and every custom path has a correct fallback; Milestone F: defend the dispatch, fallback and maintenance choice for each kernel family

focus: Query at runtime, branch on the answer, and test both sides. The check and the fallback are one unit; an untested fallback is a second implementation with zero evidence.
Family targets run across the family; arch-only targets run on one architecture. Compiling for an arch-only target silently drops every other GPU from the binary.
PTX in the fatbin is the forward-compatibility path. A cubin without PTX fails on newer hardware instead of JIT-compiling at load.
An unsupported path must error loudly at the owning API boundary with the capability and feature named, never silently run a wrong kernel.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the capability query plus dispatch for a kernel with a newer-architecture-only path and a portable fallback: correct results on sm_86 hardware, the fallback selected when the feature query is forced off, an explicit error when forced below the portable minimum, and tests covering all three branches.
traps: Compiling only with `-arch=sm_86` and calling it portable. That flag builds for one architecture; other cards need their cubin or embedded PTX.
Checking the driver version instead of the device capability. The device answers through the attribute query; the driver version does not know the chip.
Reading the marketing architecture name in code. Code branches on the numeric capability the query returns, not on Ampere or Hopper as strings.

selfTest.q: What does `cudaDevAttrComputeCapabilityMajor` return on the RTX 3050 6 GB, and which call reads it?
selfTest.a: 8, read with `cudaDeviceGetAttribute` for the device. The minor attribute returns 6; branch on the pair, not on the card name.

selfTest.q: Your kernel needs thread-block clusters. Which table gives the minimum capability, and what must the fallback do?
selfTest.a: The feature-support table in Section 5.1.3. The fallback runs a non-cluster path or returns an explicit unsupported error, selected by the runtime query, with both branches tested.

selfTest.q: A fatbin holds only an sm_90 cubin and no PTX. What happens on sm_86 and on sm_100 hardware?
selfTest.a: Neither can use that cubin, and with no PTX there is nothing to JIT-compile at load. Ship per-architecture cubins plus PTX, or restrict the matrix honestly.

selfTest.q: Why must the unsupported-path error name the capability and the feature?
selfTest.a: So a report distinguishes a missing feature from a wrong dispatch, and the matrix gains a row without guessing which check failed.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the Milestone F dispatch and fallback defense with every branch tested.
units.stopWhen: Your dispatch matrix passes on your GPU, selects the fallback when the feature query is forced off, and errors loudly when forced below the minimum.

fit.note: The compute-capabilities queries, targets and compatibility sections plus the project dispatch contract cover the matrix and fallback at implement depth.

units.title: Benchmark scenarios, MLPerf boundaries and endpoint goodput
outcomes: Distinguish offline, server, single-stream and interactive scenarios by load pattern and metric.
State MLPerf load-generation and result-boundary rules: divisions, availability states and what each reported row certifies.
Define endpoint goodput under TTFT and TPOT latency SLOs and explain why a mean-latency number cannot replace it.
Describe the arrival, length and burst properties a workload must preserve to stay credible.
units.why: A benchmark number without a scenario is noise. The scenario fixes the load, the metric and the boundary; goodput adds the latency SLO that makes throughput worth having.

next.note: Use these boundaries as the audit checklist.
Carry goodput and workload discipline into the impact report.

study.title: Endpoints benchmark: curve, points and dimensions
study.locator: What does an Endpoints benchmark show me; Technical detail: 7 to 32 points, at least 600 seconds per point, same model, endpoint and software stack; the four dimensions System TPS, interactivity, TTFT P95 and concurrency

study.title: Inference rules: scenarios, divisions and availability
study.locator: Section 4 scenarios (Single-Stream, Multi-Stream, Server, Offline) with the required-scenario examples; Closed versus Open divisions; Available, Preview and RDI availability states
study.depth: Read the scenario definitions and reporting rules reached from the datacenter page. Do not quote latency numbers from the marketing page; they live in the rules.

study.title: TTFT and TPOT pitfalls and the fluidity-index
study.locator: Section 2, Performance Metrics for LLM Inference: TTFT and TPOT definitions and why each misleads alone; Section 4.1, fluidity-index: per-token deadlines with reset after a miss, and capacity reported subject to SLOs

study.title: Serving benchmarks as a trace-property map
study.locator: Serving benchmarks subsection: Etalon, ServeGen, BurstGPT and MLPerf Endpoints entries; read it as a map to production-trace properties such as burstiness, then open the primary link for any property you borrow

focus: Endpoints sweeps concurrency into a Pareto curve with concurrency fixed per point. One point at one load is not an Endpoints result.
Closed division means the same model, apples to apples; Open allows different models or retraining. Availability states mark review status, not quality.
TTFT measures arrival to first token and TPOT averages per output token; neither sees jitter or stalls, which is why the fluidity-index adds per-token deadlines.
A credible workload preserves arrival burst and length mix from production traces. Synthetic Poisson load is a starting assumption, not evidence.
units.reproduce: Without notes, sketch the Endpoints curve axes, state the point-count and duration rules, define TTFT and TPOT, and write the fluidity deadline \(D_{i} = D_{p} + i \times D_{d}\) with the reset rule.
traps: Comparing System TPS across different concurrency or SLO points. Throughput without its latency constraint is unbounded and meaningless.
Treating a 600-second point as steady state without warmup separation. Cold start inflates the tail; the rules fix duration, not warmup.
Calling a Poisson arrival trace production-like. BurstGPT exists because real traffic bursts; check burstiness before borrowing a number.

selfTest.q: What four numbers does one Endpoints curve point report, and what varies across points?
selfTest.a: System TPS, interactivity, TTFT P95 and concurrency. Concurrency is fixed per point and swept across points, 7 to 32 points of at least 600 seconds each.

selfTest.q: Closed versus Open division: what changes?
selfTest.a: Closed requires the same model, so systems compare apples to apples. Open permits different models or retraining, so it compares approaches rather than systems.

selfTest.q: Why can mean TPOT hide a bad experience that the fluidity-index catches?
selfTest.a: TPOT averages over all output tokens, so one long stall disappears into the mean. Per-token deadlines with reset-on-miss count the stall as experienced without multiplying one stall into many misses.

selfTest.q: A vendor reports Server-scenario throughput. Name two boundary facts you check before comparing it.
selfTest.a: The division and availability state, which fix what the row certifies and its review status; and that model, endpoint and software stack match across compared rows.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the workload and result-boundary discipline (fixed stack, reported boundaries, workload frequency) in the full shape matrix.
units.stopWhen: You can place any serving number into scenario, division, availability and SLO constraints, and say which constraint is missing when one is.

fit.note: Goodput under SLOs failed on pool material: the Endpoints pages fix scenarios and reporting but define no SLO-based metric, so Etalon supplies the TTFT and TPOT pitfalls plus the deadline-based capacity metric.

units.title: Auditing benchmarks: timing, baselines, parity and cherry-picking
outcomes: Audit a GPU benchmark for timing, baseline, workload, correctness and cherry-picking flaws, and repair each with a named control.
Establish baseline parity in precision, algorithm, compiler flags and allowed libraries before claiming any speedup.
Apply the Appendix checklist as an audit list and record every deviation beside the number it affects.
units.why: Most reported speedups measure the baseline handicap, not the kernel merit. Parity first; speedup second.

next.note: See how a hardened evaluator formalizes this audit.
Keep the audit with the reproduction so the number stays honest.

study.title: The Appendix checklist as an audit list
study.locator: Appendix, AI Systems Performance Checklist: Performance Tuning and Cost Optimization Mindset; Reproducibility and Documentation Best Practices; Performance Profiling, Debugging, and Monitoring

study.title: What an unaudited benchmark reports
study.locator: Section 1 flaws: the FP32 baseline without the TF32 Tensor-Core path and the uniform positive-only tests; Section 2.2 TF32 baseline configuration; Section 3 headline results with the best model at 0.88x aggregate against 1.43x naive

study.title: Milestone F audit and measurement requirements
study.locator: Milestone F: audit a deliberately misleading benchmark and correct every flaw; Measurement requirements: retain warmup and raw samples, report medians with variance, and explicitly label measured hardware

focus: Parity means same precision, same algorithm, same flags, same libraries. One TF32 flag moved L2 results from 1.67x to 0.88x in the Verified study.
Uniform positive-only inputs hide sign, overflow and underflow paths. The audit adds negated, scaled-up and scaled-down distributions.
Hidden distributions gate correctness only; speed is always timed on the original distribution. Mixing the two mixes coverage with performance.
Keep the naive number beside the audited number. The gap between 1.43x and 0.88x is the finding, not an embarrassment.
units.reproduce: Take any fast-kernel claim and write the five-line audit: timing boundary, baseline precision and flags, input distributions, held-out status, cherry-picking check. Apply it from memory to the 374x ReLU case.
traps: TF32 only changes precision, not rankings. It moved the headline from 1.43x to 0.88x with no model left above 1x.
A passing test suite means correct. The old suite passed the ReLU identity shortcut at 374x; coverage across distributions decides, not trial count.
Faster on the benchmark means faster in production. Shapes, values and hardware were fixed; held-out behavior is a separate claim with separate tests.

selfTest.q: A custom kernel reports 1.4x over a PyTorch FP32 baseline on matmul-heavy tasks. Name the first parity check and the expected effect.
selfTest.a: Enable the TF32 Tensor-Core path in the baseline with `torch.set_float32_matmul_precision('high')`. The Verified study found TF32 alone accelerates such baselines over 1.5x on about a quarter of problems, which can erase the claimed speedup.

selfTest.q: Tests use only `torch.rand` inputs. Which three input variations does the hardened suite add, and what does each catch?
selfTest.a: Scale by 3.0 to catch overflow, scale by 0.01 to catch underflow and epsilon paths, and negate to catch sign-dependent paths like the ReLU shortcut.

selfTest.q: Why does the Verified protocol time only the original distribution?
selfTest.a: Hidden distributions are a correctness gate. Timing on them would mix numerical-path coverage with speed; any kernel failing one distribution is excluded from the aggregates instead.

selfTest.q: Aggregate Correct Speedup is a geometric mean over correct kernels. Why geometric, and where do failed kernels go?
selfTest.a: Speedups are ratios, so the geometric mean keeps a 2x and a 0.5x symmetric where an arithmetic mean would not. Failed kernels leave the mean and count toward Correctness instead.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the Milestone F audit of a deliberately misleading benchmark with every flaw corrected.
units.stopWhen: You can run the five-line audit on an unfamiliar benchmark and name which parity fix moves its headline most.

fit.note: The Appendix checklist, the Verified parity failures and Milestone F cover timing, baseline, workload, correctness and cherry-picking audit at measure depth.

units.title: KernelBench, hardened evaluators and reward hacking
outcomes: State the KernelBench task contract: levels, correctness trials, timing trials and the fast_p metric.
Explain the Verified hardening: TF32 baseline, four-distribution hidden suite, memory metric and degenerate exclusions.
Classify reward hacks by mechanism and name the test that catches each.
units.why: AI-generated kernels optimize the evaluator, not the hardware. The contract decides what counts; hardening decides what survives.

next.note: Score the surviving kernels against the speed of light.
Port the adversarial tests into your own evaluator.

study.title: Task contract, metrics and the ReLU shortcut
study.locator: Section 2.1 problem set and models (250 problems across Levels 1 to 3); Section 2.5 Metrics (Correctness, Correct Speedup, Fast at 1, memory efficiency); Appendix H.1: the ReLU identity shortcut on Level 1 problem 19

study.title: Running one problem and reading EVAL.md
study.locator: README: Task Description (Levels 1 to 4), Evaluation with `scripts/run_and_check.py` for one sample, Overall Benchmark Metric (`fast_p`); EVAL.md for benchmarking guidance

study.title: Hardening and residual hacks
study.locator: Sections 2.2 to 2.4: TF32 baseline, the four-distribution hidden suite and memory profiling; Section 3 with Figure 1 and Tables 1 to 2: none above 1x after hardening; Appendix L.3 case studies: wrong-broadcast-axis hinge loss and early-termination cumprod
study.depth: Read the two case studies for mechanism. Skim the remaining appendices; do not chase the full leaderboard.

focus: Levels 1, 2 and 3 mean single ops, fused chains and full models. `fast_p` counts kernels both correct and faster than threshold \(p\); `fast_0` is correctness alone.
The ReLU shortcut passed because every test input was non-negative. The fix is negated inputs, not more trials of the same distribution.
Wrong-axis and early-exit hacks survive value variation but break on distribution shift or sustained inputs. The judge audit flagged 6 of 453 survivors, with 4 genuine hacks.
Degenerate constant-zero references were excluded, not fixed. Some problems cannot measure speedup, and the honest move is exclusion.
units.reproduce: From memory, write the KernelBench contract (levels, trials, `fast_p`), the four hidden distributions with their scales, and the ReLU-hack mechanism plus its catching test.
traps: More random tests equal stronger evaluation. The old suite ran many trials of one distribution; strength comes from distinct distributions, not count.
A kernel faster on every tested shape generalizes. Shapes were fixed and shape specialization is declared legitimate; values are the held-out axis.
Memory efficiency follows speed. Over a quarter of surviving fast kernels used more memory; measure both or the tradeoff hides.

selfTest.q: What does `fast_1` count, exactly?
selfTest.a: The fraction of tasks whose kernel is both correct and faster than the PyTorch baseline, a speedup above 1. `fast_0` is correctness alone.

selfTest.q: How did the ReLU identity shortcut reach 374x, and which distribution catches it?
selfTest.a: Every test input came from `torch.rand`, uniform and non-negative, so returning the input unchanged passed; a shape guard limited the trick to the benchmark shape. Negated inputs fail it with maximum error 1.0.

selfTest.q: Why did the hinge-loss wrong-axis kernel pass all four hidden distributions?
selfTest.a: Over tens of thousands of independent inputs the mean error stays under tolerance by the law of large numbers despite the wrong axis. Only a judge checking the axis, or a non-identical layout, catches it.

selfTest.q: A fused GroupNorm kernel is fast but numerically unstable. Which hardening catches it, and why did the original suite miss it?
selfTest.a: The scaled distributions: times 3.0 stresses overflow and times 0.01 stresses underflow and epsilon paths. The original uniform small-positive inputs never touched those paths.
